This is the 1996 translation by Malcolm Heath, the Penguin Classics edition. There are many others. This one has a cover that, unlike a lot of Penguin's choices for their reissues, actually makes you smile a little: it's a picture of a small theatre surrounded by dancing clowns, actors, actresses, audiences ... but the curtain is pulled back on a man sitting quietly and smiling as he reads a book. That's Aristotle, studying at the heart of the theatre. It's nice to get a plain statement of the theme of the book on its cover.

I was attracted to Poetics because its name is all but whispered in writing circles: the "Aristotlean three act structure", the "bedrock of literary criticism", the "Aristotlean guide to tragedy." Maybe the thing that made me most curious about it was that Robert McKee's book Story is said to be a modern updating of the book. I think it's important to at least look up the foundations of the thought or belief systems that we have to hand, mainly because a lot of shit often gets attributed to people who didn't actually say it, or books are often worshipped without actually realising what they maintain.

That said, the most instructive and useful part of the book was Heath's introduction. It is longer than the actual text of Poetics itself. Part of this is because Poetics is not a complete document: it is a fragment, a collection of lecture notes by Aristotle on the subject specifically of tragedy and historical epic. (It is conjectured that Aristotle did write a second, long text on the art of comedy -- this fictional text is at the heart of Umberto Eco's lovely story The Name of the Rose, but we have not recovered any such text). Either way, Poetics is not a full text, and at best it's a summary of lessons.

But the introduction is also very important since it provides much-needed context for Aristotle's remarks. It does a lot to demystify and ground us in what the notes are and how far you can take their insights.

I distilled two major themes from Heath's introduction.

First and foremost, Poetics is a philosophical text - just as with his other works, Rhetoric, The Politics, and The Nicomachean Ethics.

This is not to imply any failure on Aristotle's part. Like a good mathematician, he sets out his foundational assumptions and premises at the start of Poetics, i.e. why tragedy or drama in general works. His foundation is: human beings enjoy imitation, or representation. An imitation or representation -- and here we first get into translation issues, ancient Greek is not fully translatable to English -- is to create something that causes a person to understand that thing as something in nature. For example, when we look at the Mona Lisa, we see an imitation or representation of a woman. Aristotle holds that this leap of understanding causes human beings pleasure, because human beings enjoy understanding things. Therefore we enjoy looking at the Mona Lisa. When we watch a drama, or a tragedy, we are looking at the imitation or representation of a series of events, a complete chain from beginning to end. This causes us pleasure because we understand that to be representation of a series of events, and certain elements within that drama will cause us fear and pity.

Every observation Aristotle makes from that point on rests on that foundation. Again, for this Aristotle is to be applauded: it's essentially a means by which you can 'check your math'. But it also makes Poetics feel a lot like an entomologist's glass-fronted display box: full of beautiful butterflies and clearly displaying the wonderful colours of their wings, but every last one stone dead. Aristotle does recognise this. He says certain skills -- particularly metaphor, perhaps the supreme mode of imitation or representation -- simply cannot be taught, that the best metaphors are created by the naturally talented or the mad.

The second, and just as important, point that comes out of Heath's introduction is that Aristotle is speaking to his own time and his own culture's idea of tragedy. I suspect a lot of writers come at Poetics in the same way that businessmen, strategists, generals, etc, etc, come at Sun Tzu's The Art of War: plunge right into the text without considering the translation or considering the context of the book in its own time. And Poetics is very clearly (again, through no fault of Aristotle's) written towards a specific area of endeavour: the Greek form of tragedy as played for audiences in the Peloppenese three hundred years before the birth of Christ.

This form of drama was very, very different to those we have today. There was still a chorus; there were only one or two actors; there wasn't anything like modern film; women and slaves were famously thought to be of inferior character generally to men; actors still all spoke in rhythmic verse and song for whole plays.

Sure, you can say "B-b-but he was speaking to the heart of drama!" Sure. Perhaps he was. But that's like saying an ornithologist has meaningful, practical advice to offer to a modern-day aerospace engineer who builds 747s. Yes, in theory they have something in common, but the commonalities are so basic that the aerospace engineer is going to master the relevant common skillset on the way to making something that weighs hundreds of tons actually get off the ground and land again safely. And in no world would we seriously tell the aerospace engineer that the ornithologist has said all there is to know about flight.

Coming back to "Aristotlean three-act structure". Spoiler alert: there isn't one. Greek drama didn't operate in acts. That's a more modern invention. Aristotle's only word on the subject of "three acts" is as follows:

Now, according to our definition Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is complete, and whole, and of a certain magnitude; for there may be a whole that is wanting in magnitude. A whole is that which has a beginning, a middle, and an end. A beginning is that which does not itself follow anything by causal necessity, but after which something naturally is or comes to be. An end, on the contrary, is that which itself naturally follows some other thing, either by necessity, or as a rule, but has nothing following it. A middle is that which follows something as some other thing follows it. A well constructed plot, therefore, must neither begin nor end at haphazard, but conform to these principles.

That's it. Note again the fact this proposition depends on Aristotle's first assumptions that imitation is what we find pleasurable. This text is just saying you can't have a story without it starting, continuing, and ending -- because whole things in life have a beginning, a middle, and an end, and art is imitation of something we find in life. A brick has a beginning, middle, and an end. It's not divided into three separate bricks which are bonded together. Aristotle's remarks have far more to do with causality of events in fiction than they do arbitrarily carving up a story into three parts.

Insofar as Aristotle saw a tragedy having "acts", he divided the drama in two pieces: before the disaster that befalls the hero and after that disaster. Yet for centuries we have been told Aristotle created the idea of three acts.

On the other hand, Aristotle probably has the same insight and the same things to say about modern characters and modern plots as half a hundred how-to-write authors do. Aristotle at least is rigorous about "showin' his work", so to speak, in that you can clearly see his reasoning. Very few other authors or gurus in this field do. Aristotle has the advantage of logic to his conclusions, even if the premise is arbitrary. And the advice is still a root fundamental for much of the "advice" current writing gurus give us, if one is prepared to take Aristotle's words and interpret them for our time. I therefore don't disendorse the book: on the contrary, Aristotle's logic is glittering if not dazzling, and some of his fundamental ideas about plot and character have carried down to our own time. But neither is he the be-all and end-all of how to write a good story. As he said: metaphor is the talent of the gifted or the mad. All art, I think, depends on a little madness, and notwithstanding roughly 150 years of modern psychoanalysis, you can't teach madness any more than you can teach giftedness. The book is worth a read, if only to disabuse yourself of some of the claims made of its greatness.
